01Crown HoursShift & pay tracker

My shifts always change. I didn't even know if I got the right pay.

The pain
Hospitality rosters change all the time, so the hours I actually work rarely match the original roster. I had no easy way to check my pay was right.
What I built
A shift tracker built with Claude. An 11 PM reminder nudges me, I log the shift in seconds (normal, sick, holiday or day off), and it works out paid hours after breaks, flags overtime and builds a timecard check for every fortnight.
The outcome
When my payslip arrives, I compare it with my time log, spot any day that's missing pay and chase it up. No more hours quietly disappearing.
Prototype in Figma
I connected Claude to Figma to map the whole app as a clickable prototype flow, screen by screen.

Case study · Business Analysis
Capstone · Curtin University

Smart Project Recommendation System

A web-based system that matches final-year students to the right project and supervisor, using an LLM and the SFIA skills framework.

Business requirementsSoftware product lifecycleLLMFigmaER design
3user roles
32business requirements
12database tables
1skills framework (SFIA)
▶ Watch the prototype: role select, student recommendations, supervisor projects, admin dashboard

The problem

Final-semester students lose weeks at the very start of their graduate project, choosing a topic and finding a supervisor who fits.

⏳ Slow topic selection

Students spend weeks searching for a suitable topic, delaying the whole project.

📅 Supervisor mismatch

Scheduling conflicts, and student interests that don't match the supervisor's expertise.

🧭 No clear direction

Students meet supervisors without a defined interest, so meetings go in circles.

Impact: lost time, late starts, and wasted student and supervisor hours, which ends up hurting project quality.

The solution

A web-based Project Recommendation System with two jobs:

For supervisors

Publish and advertise ready-made project topics.

For students

Get topics recommended from their enrolled units, grades and interests, with a match score.

Both projects and student profiles are mapped to SFIA (Skills Framework for the Information Age), so matches are compared on one shared skills language.

Who uses it

Three actors: students create a profile, view project recommendations and book an appointment with a supervisor; project supervisors create projects, update project status and confirm appointments; administrators maintain the website and manage projects, supervisors and students. Everyone starts at the same login.

Prototype

I mapped every screen in Figma, from login through the student, supervisor and admin flows, then built the clickable mock-up shown at the top of this page.

Business requirements

32 testable requirements across 11 modules, covering happy paths and error handling (invalid logins, failed transcript uploads, missing required fields, no matches found). Tap a module to see its requirements.

Database design

From the business requirements and use cases I designed the relational model as an ER diagram: students, courses, units and enrolments on one side, projects and supervisors on the other, linked through SFIA skill maps so units and projects can be scored against the same skills.

What this shows: turning a messy real problem into clear requirements, a flow every role can follow, and a data model developers can build from.
Case study · Data Visualisation
Tableau · Financial analysis

Analysis & Visualisation of CSL

An interactive Tableau dashboard on the financial performance of CSL Ltd., a leading biotechnology company, built to support data-driven decisions with historical and forecasted insights.

TableauFinancial KPIsForecastingDashboard design
Open the interactive dashboard on Tableau Public ↗

About the project

The dashboard analyses the financial performance of CSL Ltd., highlighting key indicators such as revenue growth, net income, EBITDA, earnings per share and retained earnings over time. Its goal is to support data-driven decision making with both historical and forecasted financial insights.

Key components

📈 Revenues & Profits

Total revenue against net profit margin across decades, showing profitability trends.

🔮 Forecast Analysis

Predictive modelling for future net income (e.g. +7% growth in 2024) to aid investor and strategic planning.

🧾 Expense Composition

Expense categories (e.g. R&D, depreciation) over the last 10 years to track operational focus.

🏦 Retained Earnings

Retained earnings growth relative to profit, showing the company's reinvestment strategy.

🎯 KPI Cards

Quick year-over-year summaries, including dividends per share and EBITDA.

Case study · Data Visualisation
Tableau · 3-page dashboard

Analysis & Visualisation of Samsung

A comprehensive financial analysis of Samsung in a three-page interactive Tableau dashboard, turning historical financial data into visual insights on performance trends, cost structures and future forecasts.

TableauFinancial analysisForecastingData storytelling
Open the interactive dashboard on Tableau Public ↗

About the project

This project presents a comprehensive financial analysis of Samsung using a three-page interactive dashboard built in Tableau. It translates historical financial data into actionable visual insights, so users can explore company performance trends, cost structures and future forecasts.

Page 1: Company's Overview

  • Summarises average financial indicators (Revenue, EBITDA, Net Income, Dividends and Margin) for any selected year.
  • Provides background context, including Samsung's strategic direction and business purpose.
  • Includes a dynamic income table for year-over-year comparison and a line chart of revenue vs. profit growth from 1997 to 2023.

Page 2: Cost & Income Analysis

  • Compares total revenues vs. expenses, showing the resulting net income trends.
  • Breaks down EBITDA, Gross Profit and Net Income margins with donut charts.
  • Tracks Net Income Margin Growth over decades.
  • Includes an expense composition bar chart highlighting major cost categories like Cost of Goods Sold, R&D and Operating Expenses.

Page 3: Investor Insights & Forecast Analysis

  • Highlights retained earnings trends and Samsung's reinvestment strategy.
  • Presents key investor metrics like EPS, EBIT, Dividends and Payout Ratio.
  • Offers forecasting: users pick a financial indicator (e.g. EBIT) and predict values up to 2027.
  • Visualises gains and losses from assets and investments and net interest gain/loss trends.

Conclusion

Based on this analysis, Samsung appears to be a strong candidate for long-term investment: consistent revenue and profit growth, a stable net income margin, and a clear commitment to reinvestment, seen in its growing retained earnings.

Through this project I further developed my skills in data storytelling, financial analysis and dashboard design in Tableau, and saw how well-designed visuals help people make informed, data-driven decisions.

Case study · New Product Design
Product development · Curtin University

Bloody Help: Click-to-Remove Magic Pen

A portable, pen-shaped detergent that erases menstrual stains in seconds, with no water and no full wash. Tagline: “Confidence in your pocket.”

Product designMarket sizingGo-to-marketProject planning
Watch the proposal pitch on YouTube ↗

About the project

Bloody Help is a portable detergent in a pen-shaped package, built for convenient, travel-friendly cleaning on any day of the menstrual cycle. It removes menstrual stains in a few seconds without water or a full laundry cycle.

The formula stays gentle on skin with enzyme-based protein technology that prevents irritation. The pen is also refillable: users keep the outer case and replace only the detergent, which cuts waste and lowers packaging cost.

The problem

  • Every month, period stains cost people school days, confidence during the day, and time spent on special laundry.
  • On average, 11 school days are missed per year.
  • The solution: remove blood stains without water or washing, in a compact, portable and refillable, eco-friendly design.

Product concept & design decisions

Options weighed during development:

  • Scope: remove all stain types, or focus on menstrual stains only? We chose menstrual stains first, to enter a clearly defined market.
  • Dispensing: a squeeze gel tube was easy to aim, but hard to control per use and prone to leaks. We chose a click mechanism that dispenses a controlled amount each time.
  • Size: compact with fewer uses, or larger and less portable? We kept it small enough to carry daily.
  • Applicator: a brush tip could absorb stains back and grow bacteria, so we switched to stainless steel, which is easy to clean after use.
  • Refill system: reuse the outer case and replace only the detergent, so it's cheaper for customers, cheaper to produce, and less waste.

Prototype testing plan

  • Stain removal performance: fresh stains, then 5 min, 30 min, 1 hour and 24 hours, measuring cleanliness.
  • Click mechanism: consistent detergent per click and the number of uses per pen.
  • Leakage & durability: after first seal, during transport, on mechanical failure, and carried in pockets, pencil cases and purses.
  • Irritation test: synthetic skin, to confirm ingredients are gentle.

Uniqueness & market

1.5 BTotal available market: general detergents
100 MServiceable market: detergent specifically for blood stains
25 MOur share: portable stain remover
  • Primary market, teenagers: new to feminine hygiene products, with active lifestyles like sport.
  • Secondary market, working women: office workers sit for long periods (high leak risk), and outdoor workers find it hard to change pads or tampons during work.

Business model & go-to-market

Mission: become the essential personal care item every woman carries during her cycle: reliable, gentle, convenient and eco-friendly.

  • Revenue: full-pen sales plus refills. Refill volume doubles as a signal of market acceptance and brand loyalty.
  • Pricing: penetration pricing, so it's affordable for students and low-risk to try.
  • Channels: launch on TikTok and YouTube for young women, plus free samples through schools and universities to gather direct feedback. Sold online and through retailers like Coles and Woolworths.
  • Logistics: online orders ship from the main warehouse via Australia Post, with QR-code returns; retail stock flows through distribution centres to stores.

Project milestones

A 10-month plan from market research in January to launch in September, with alpha testing, a redesign and a user beta trial before full manufacturing.

What this shows: taking a product from a real everyday problem to a tested concept, a sized market, a business model and a delivery plan.
